notes.meaning: Paul introduces Phoebe and asks the believers in Rome to give her a warm reception. She was a member of the church at Cenchrea, a port near Corinth, and served the congregation faithfully as a helper or deacon. She was likely the trusted person who carried this letter all the way to Rome.

differ.view: Methodists traditionally hold that Phoebe held an official church office as a deaconess who cared for the sick and ministered to women.
Many Baptists understand her title in a general sense as a devoted servant using her own means, not an ordained church officer.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Catholic tradition recognizes Phoebe as a ministering woman who assisted in caring for the poor and helping with the baptism of women.

notes.meaning: Paul urges the Roman church to welcome Phoebe as a sister in Christ and to give her any help she needs for her business. He explains that she has been a generous patron and helper to many believers, including Paul himself. Christians should always be ready to care for those who have spent their lives helping others.

Paul sends greetings to Prisca and Aquila, a married couple who worked closely with him to share the good news of Jesus. Prisca is mentioned first, which suggests she was energetic and well known in the work of the church. They had labored with Paul in Corinth and Ephesus and were now living back in Rome.

This brave couple had risked their own lives to protect Paul during a time of extreme danger. Because of their sacrifice, not only Paul but all the Gentile churches were deeply thankful to them. Their willingness to face death showed their deep love for Christ and His messengers.

Paul sends greetings to the group of believers who met for worship in the home of Prisca and Aquila. Early Christians did not have dedicated church buildings, so they gathered in private houses. He also greets Epenetus, a dear friend who was the very first person in the Roman province of Asia to trust in Christ.

Paul greets Mary, a Christian woman in Rome who worked tirelessly for the believers there. Although Scripture tells us little else about her life, Paul honors her quiet, hard work in the church. God notices and remembers all faithful service done for His people.

Paul greets Andronicus and Junia, who were fellow Jews and had shared prison with him for preaching the gospel. They became followers of Jesus even before Paul did, and they were held in high honor among the missionaries. Paul humbly acknowledges that these faithful saints walked with Christ before he did.

differ.view: Some evangelicals understand the word apostle here in a broader sense of traveling messenger, meaning this couple served faithfully as notable church workers rather than holding the apostolic office.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Many modern scholars understand Junia to be a woman who was recognized as an outstanding apostle in her own right, while others translate the phrase to mean well known to the apostles.

notes.meaning: Paul sends a warm greeting to Ampliatus, whom he describes as his beloved brother in the Lord. This simple message shows Paul's deep personal affection for ordinary Christians who were steadfast in faith. Even without famous titles, believers are precious to God and to one another.

Paul greets Urbanus, calling him a fellow worker in the service of Christ, along with his dear friend Stachys. Urbanus worked alongside other believers to help spread the gospel, while Stachys was specially loved by Paul. True Christian friendship flourishes as believers serve Jesus together.

Paul greets Apelles, whose faith had been tested and proven genuine through trials. He also sends greetings to the believers who belonged to the household of Aristobulus. Even when the master of a house was not a believer, servants and family members could still form a thriving Christian group.

Paul greets Herodion, a fellow Jewish countryman, and sends his love to the believers in the household of Narcissus. Only those in that house who were in the Lord are greeted, showing that faith in Christ is a personal choice. Family connections cannot save a person, but God calls individuals out of pagan homes into His light.

Paul sends greetings to Tryphena and Tryphosa, two women who worked diligently in serving the Lord. He also greets Persis, another faithful woman who had worked especially hard for the gospel. Paul gladly recognized the essential role women played in building up the early church.

Paul greets Rufus, an outstanding Christian chosen by the Lord, and greets Rufus's mother, who had treated Paul like her own son. This Rufus may have been the son of Simon of Cyrene, the man who was forced to carry Jesus' cross. Christian love creates family bonds that are as real and tender as biological families.

Paul greets a group of believers named Asyncritus, Phlegon, Hermes, Patrobas, and Hermas, along with the brothers gathered with them. These names were common among servants and working people in Rome, showing that the church included ordinary citizens. Paul remembered and valued every believer, no matter their social rank.

Paul greets Philologus, Julia, Nereus and his sister, Olympas, and all the saints gathered with them. The word saints means people set apart by God to belong to Him. These believers likely formed another small house church meeting in a different part of the city.

Paul instructs the Roman Christians to greet each other with a holy kiss, a customary cultural greeting used in that time to show sincere love. He adds that all the churches of Christ join him in sending their warm greetings. Believers across different cities and nations belong to one united family in Christ.

Paul urges the believers to keep a sharp watch for people who cause divisions and place stumbling blocks in front of others. These troublemakers taught ideas that contradicted the true gospel the church had learned from the apostles. The command is simple and direct: stay away from them to protect the unity and peace of the church.

People who stir up strife do not truly serve Christ, but their own selfish desires and worldly appetites. They use smooth words and flattering compliments to win people's trust and trick unsuspecting believers. Christians must be on guard because false teachers often sound pleasant and convincing on the outside.

Paul rejoices because the Roman believers already had a great reputation everywhere for being obedient to the faith. Yet he warns them to be wise about what is good and innocent about what is evil. Christians should have a deep grasp of God's truth while remaining unstained and inexperienced in wickedness.

Paul promises that the God of peace will soon crush Satan under the believers' feet, echoing God's ancient promise in the Garden of Eden. God Himself wins the victory over evil, but He shares that triumph with His faithful church. Paul closes this warning with a prayer that the grace of Jesus will be with them all.

differ.view: Some Baptists emphasize that this victory looks ahead primarily to the final judgment at the return of Christ when Satan is banished forever.
Reformed writers teach that while Christ won the decisive battle on the cross, this promise also guarantees ongoing, present victories over the devil's schemes in the church's daily struggles.

notes.meaning: Paul passes along greetings from Timothy, his trusted co-worker who was helping him in Corinth. Greetings also come from Lucius, Jason, and Sosipater, who were Paul's Jewish countrymen. These companions shared in Paul's missionary work and wanted the Roman believers to know of their love and fellowship.

Tertius, the scribe whom Paul used to write down the letter, adds his own personal greeting in the Lord. Ancient writers often dictated letters to a skilled secretary, and Paul gladly allowed Tertius to greet the Roman church directly. Even behind-the-scenes helpers are honored as true partners in ministry.

Gaius sends greetings as the generous homeowner hosting both Paul and the whole local church in Corinth. Erastus, the city treasurer of Corinth, and Quartus, a Christian brother, also send their love. This shows that the early church brought together people from all walks of life, including public officials and ordinary citizens.

This verse repeats the blessing wishing the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ to be with all the readers. The earliest and most reliable Greek manuscripts do not contain this verse, as scribes likely copied the blessing from verse twenty to create a traditional closing.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Modern textual scholars note that verse 24 is absent from the oldest manuscripts and was likely added later as a repeating benediction.

notes.meaning: Paul directs praise to God, who has the power to make believers stand strong in the faith through the preaching about Jesus Christ. This gospel reveals God's mystery, which means His eternal plan of salvation that was once hidden from human understanding. God establishes our hearts not by our own strength, but by the good news of His Son.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some ancient manuscripts place this closing song of praise at the end of chapter 14 or chapter 15, though scholars agree it forms an authentic part of Romans.

notes.meaning: God's secret plan has now been unveiled through the writings of the Old Testament prophets and the preaching of the apostles. By the command of the eternal God, this message is being announced to all nations so people everywhere may trust and obey Him. God's purpose has always been to welcome Gentiles and Jews into one family through faith.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some ancient manuscripts place this closing song of praise at the end of chapter 14 or chapter 15, though scholars agree it forms an authentic part of Romans.

notes.meaning: Paul ends the entire letter by giving glory forever to the only wise God through Jesus Christ. God's marvelous wisdom planned salvation and brought Jews and Gentiles together in one body. Everything in the Christian life leads back to praising God for His greatness and mercy.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some ancient manuscripts place this closing song of praise at the end of chapter 14 or chapter 15, though scholars agree it forms an authentic part of Romans.
